title: Did These Microbes Eat A Lot of the Fossil Record? - Nautilus
gist: The fossil record is biased toward hard parts, yet soft-bodied organisms of the late Ediacaran period (579 to 539 million years ago) left abundant fossils; a new Current Biology study may explain this long-standing mystery.

insights.claim: The fossil record is biased because soft tissues such as organs are very rarely preserved, leaving paleontologists to reconstruct extinct life mainly from bones, shells and exoskeletons.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Sampling bias in the historical record can systematically distort conclusions, a general lesson for any dataset-driven inference.
insights.quote: Because soft tissues like organs are very rarely preserved, paleontologists are left to piece together extinct life from the hard stuff (bones, shells, exoskeletons, etc.).

insights.claim: During the late Ediacaran period, between 579 and 539 million years ago, newly evolved complex organisms were mostly soft-bodied yet left plentiful fossils, sometimes preserving entire ecosystems.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: An anomaly in preservation conditions that suggests environmental factors once differed sharply from today.
insights.quote: the newly evolved complex organisms were mostly squishy. And yet, they left plenty of fossils behind—sometimes entire alien-like ecosystems.

insights.claim: A new study published in Current Biology may explain why Ediacaran soft-bodied organisms were so well preserved, with the article's framing pointing to microbes and polymer degradation as the factor.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Resolution of the puzzle could reshape understanding of early complex life and the reliability of the fossil record.
insights.quote: now a new study published in Current Biology may have finally cracked the case
